title: Supernova Remnant LMC N132D
caption: Supernova remnant N132D in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: LMC N132D, SNR J052501-693842 · constellation Dorado · about 170,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble SM4 ERO Team

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Hubble shows N132D, the remains of a star that exploded as a supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way. The remnant lies about 170,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Dorado. A supernova remnant is the expanding cloud of debris left behind by the blast, along with the surrounding gas that it sweeps up and heats.

The image combines exposures from two Hubble cameras taken years apart. The Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in January 2004, and the newly installed Wide Field Camera 3 added data in August 2009. Some filters capture broad bands of starlight, while narrow ones isolate the glow of hydrogen, nitrogen and sulfur in the remnant's gas.

NASA released the picture in September 2009 among the first views from Hubble after the STS-125 servicing mission in May. That mission installed Wide Field Camera 3 and repaired the Advanced Camera for Surveys, and NASA described the telescope as more powerful than it had ever been.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys combined five filters. NASA shows F475W (g) in blue, F550M (y) in green, F658N (hydrogen-alpha plus nitrogen) in orange, F673N (sulfur) in white and F850LP (z) in pink.
understand.eye: The narrow filters pick out the glow of particular elements one at a time, and the F850LP filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: Astronauts also installed the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph and repaired the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph on the same mission. According to NASA, the new instruments were more sensitive to light, letting Hubble finish observations in a fraction of the time older instruments needed.
